params.question: Which of the following BEST distinguishes intellectual disability from global developmental delay?

answers.text: Global developmental delay applies to children above 5 years, while intellectual disability applies below 5 years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. It is the other way round. GDD is used for children under 5 who show delay in two or more developmental domains. Intellectual disability is formally diagnosed from age 5 onwards after standardised IQ testing.

answers.text: Global developmental delay requires formal IQ testing, whereas intellectual disability is a purely clinical observation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. GDD is a clinical observation of delay in multiple domains. It is intellectual disability that requires formal IQ testing — specifically an IQ below 70 — along with documented adaptive functioning deficits.

answers.text: Intellectual disability requires an IQ below 70 with adaptive deficits and is formally diagnosed from age 5, whereas GDD refers to delay in two or more domains in children under 5

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. GDD is used when a child under 5 shows delay in two or more developmental domains. Intellectual disability is reserved for age 5 and above, requiring a formally tested IQ below 70 plus significant adaptive functioning deficits, with onset before age 18.

answers.text: Intellectual disability always involves motor delay, whereas global developmental delay does not

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Intellectual disability is defined by cognitive and adaptive deficits, not specifically motor delay. Both GDD and intellectual disability can involve motor delay, but it is not a defining requirement of either.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the key distinction: GDD describes delay in ≥2 domains in children under 5, while intellectual disability requires IQ <70 plus adaptive deficits, formally confirmed from age 5 onwards.

Well done. Remembering that GDD is a clinical label for young children while intellectual disability is a formal diagnosis after age 5 will help you communicate accurately with families and colleagues.

params.question: A 2-year-old girl presents with delayed walking and no speech. Her mother has been advised to see a neurologist, a speech therapist, and a psychologist separately over the next three months. What is the BEST alternative recommendation?

answers.text: Refer to a Child Developmental Unit where all specialists assess the child in a single coordinated visit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The CDU brings physiotherapy, speech therapy, psychology, and developmental paediatrics together in one visit. Each professional contributes a unique perspective, and the developmental paediatrician integrates all observations into a single coherent diagnosis and management plan — far more efficient and accurate than scattered sequential appointments.

answers.text: See the neurologist first and defer other specialist referrals until that evaluation is complete

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Sequential single-specialist visits delay the comprehensive picture. No single professional can capture the whole child alone — the CDU model avoids this by assessing motor, language, cognitive, and behavioural domains simultaneously.

answers.text: Skip specialist referrals and begin physiotherapy immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While physiotherapy may eventually be needed for motor delay, starting treatment without a comprehensive multidisciplinary assessment risks missing the underlying cause and co-existing problems such as hearing loss or autism spectrum features.

answers.text: Wait until the child turns three, since many children catch up on their own

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A 2-year-old with both motor and language delay warrants prompt evaluation. Early intervention during the first two to three years — when the brain is most adaptable — leads to significantly better outcomes than a watch-and-wait approach.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key advantage of a CDU is that the entire multidisciplinary team — physiotherapist, speech therapist, psychologist, and developmental paediatrician — assesses the child together in one visit, producing one coordinated plan.
Exactly right. The CDU's integrated model gives a more accurate diagnosis and a better experience for the family than fragmented referrals.

interactions.label: Which statement about the diagnosis of ADHD is correct according to DSM-5?

params.question: Which statement about the diagnosis of ADHD is correct according to DSM-5?

answers.text: ADHD can be diagnosed when symptoms are present in a single setting, provided they are severe

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Severity in one setting alone is not sufficient. The DSM-5 requires symptoms to be present in more than one setting — this cross-setting requirement ensures the difficulty is pervasive rather than situational.

answers.text: The predominantly inattentive presentation is always diagnosed earlier than the hyperactive-impulsive type

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The predominantly inattentive presentation is actually the most commonly missed, especially in girls, because these children are not disruptive and do not attract classroom attention. The hyperactive-impulsive presentation is far more visible and gets referred sooner.

answers.text: Hyperactivity must be the dominant symptom for an ADHD diagnosis to be made

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. ADHD has three recognised presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined. A child with the inattentive presentation shows primarily attentional difficulties with minimal hyperactivity and still meets diagnostic criteria.

answers.text: ADHD symptoms must be present in more than one setting, such as both at home and at school

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The DSM-5 requires ADHD symptoms to be present across multiple settings. A child who struggles only at school but not at home does not meet the diagnostic threshold. This cross-setting requirement distinguishes ADHD from situation-specific problems like a difficult classroom environment.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: ADHD symptoms must appear in more than one setting (e.g. home and school). A child who struggles only at school does not meet DSM-5 criteria for ADHD.
Well done. The cross-setting rule is one of the most clinically important DSM-5 criteria — it prevents mislabelling situational difficulties as ADHD.

interactions.label: The presence of eye contact and some spoken language rules out a diagnosis of au

params.question: The presence of eye contact and some spoken language rules out a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. Autism is a spectrum — some children with ASD do make eye contact and use spoken words. The DSM-5 diagnosis requires persistent deficits in both social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviour domains. It is not ruled out by the presence of any single skill. The narration specifically warns that dismissing ASD because a child has some language or eye contact is a common clinical mistake.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Autism is a spectrum with wide variation in presentation. Many children with ASD make some eye contact and have partial spoken language. Diagnosis rests on persistent deficits across both core domains (social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviours), not on the absence of any single skill. Ruling out ASD solely because a child speaks or makes eye contact is a recognised clinical pitfall that delays diagnosis.

params.question: A 2-year-old with global developmental delay has been diagnosed with significant lead poisoning. Which management step should take FIRST priority?

answers.text: Begin a phenylalanine-restricted diet to prevent further neurotoxic damage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A phenylalanine-restricted diet is the specific management for phenylketonuria, not lead poisoning. Each treatable cause has its own targeted intervention — lead poisoning requires chelation therapy.

answers.text: Start chelation therapy to treat the identified toxic cause before adding developmental therapies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When a specific treatable cause of developmental delay is identified, treating it takes first priority. For significant lead poisoning, chelation therapy removes the ongoing toxic exposure. Developmental therapies such as physiotherapy and speech therapy are important but come after addressing the underlying cause.

answers.text: Enrol the child in speech therapy as the immediate first step

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While speech therapy is valuable for language delay, the immediate priority when a treatable cause like lead poisoning is identified is to treat that cause first. Ongoing toxic exposure continues to damage the developing brain until addressed.

answers.text: Refer to a Child Developmental Unit for comprehensive evaluation before starting any treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This child already has a confirmed diagnosis with an identified treatable cause. The priority is to act on that cause — chelation therapy for lead poisoning — rather than delaying treatment for further evaluation.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a specific treatable cause is found — whether congenital hypothyroidism, PKU, or lead poisoning — treating it comes first. For lead poisoning, that means chelation therapy before layering on developmental therapies.
Exactly right. 'Treat any cause we can treat' is the first principle of developmental delay management — and timing matters, especially during the early years when the brain is most adaptable.
